newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. staff listed U.S. Iraq strikes as violations.
newsitem.headline: U.N. staff listed U.S. Iraq strikes as violations.

text.p: U.N. observers reported some U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq this month as a violation of the demilitarised zone between Iraq and Kuwait set up by the United Nations after the Gulf War, a U.N. official said on Wednesday.

The official of the U.N. Iraq-Kuwait Observer Mission (UNIKOM) told Reuters eight of the 44 cruise missiles fired at Iraq by U.S. forces in the Gulf on September 3 and 4 were seen by UNIKOM observers as they flew over the zone on their way north to targets in Iraq.

The official said the observers registered the eight missiles as a violation of the demilitarised status of the frontier enshrined in U.N. resolutions passed after the conflict ended a seven-month Iraqi occupation of Kuwait in February 1991.
The violations were reported to U.N. headquarters in New York, the UNIKOM official said.
The United Nations created the demilitarised border zone in April 1991 and deployed UNIKOM along it to monitor the boundary and help deter any violations of it by either side.
UNIKOM's observers try to ensure that no military activity of any kind occurs in the zone that straddles the 207 km (130 mile)-long land border and 40 km (25 mile)-sea border.
They must also ensure that no military force of any kind is present in the zone, which extends 10 km (six miles) into Iraq and five km (three miles) into Kuwait.

The UNIKOM official said it was impossible to verify the nationality of the forces that fired the eight missiles but added it appeared they were among the 44 launched by the United States as punishment for Iraqi attacks on northern Iraqi Kurds.
"Any overflights over the DMZ (demilitarised zone) by either side, or by their allies, constitutes a violation," said UNIKOM spokesman Saleem Fahmawi.

Fahamawi added that the situation in the zone was calm and no other significant military movements had been noticed during the latest flare-up between Washington and Iraq over the enforcement of a Western-imposed no-fly zone in southern Iraq.
In Kuwait, a senior diplomat said: "We have no clear evidence of any ground force movements by Iraq that have constituted an immediate threat to Kuwait."
Western diplomats said they did not expect a diplomatic indicent over the UNIKOM report, describing it as "theoretical" and said it had not been an issue at U.N. headquarters.
"If there are violations of the boundary on the ground, these can be fairly easily redressed. But is difficult to see what can done about the missiles so it just isn't an issue," one diplomat said.
Diplomats said they believed some U.S. missile strikes against Iraq during previous confrontations with Baghdad in 1993 and 1994 had also been reported as violations by UNIKOM.
The U.N. official said UNIKOM observers also saw two unidentified warplanes making a rare low flight over the demilitarised zone on Wednesday and planned to report this as a violation of the zone.
Witnesses said the planes appeared to be Western aircraft participating in patrols of a no-fly zone imposed in southern Iraq by the United States, France and Britain in 1992.
Diplomats say the patrols are normally not an issue for UNIKOM because they usually fly too high to be seen by the observers, who rely on the naked eye for surveillance.

UNIKOM has described the most common violations of the zone as the carrying of illegal weapons into the zone, incursions by unauthorised small groups of military personel, illegal border crossings by civilians and overflights by military aircraft -- presumably a reference to Southern Watch flights.
